articles.title: Growing potatoes in a container
articles.summary: A manageable way to grow a small crop where garden space is limited.
articles.body:
Choose a sturdy container with drainage holes and enough room for roots. Use certified seed potatoes from a garden supplier rather than supermarket potatoes.

1. Add 10 to 15 cm of compost. Place two or three chitted seed potatoes on top, shoots facing up, then cover with another 10 cm.
2. Water to settle the compost and keep it evenly moist. Containers dry faster than garden beds, especially in wind and warm weather. Do not leave the pot standing in water.
3. As leafy shoots grow, add compost around the stems in stages, leaving the top leaves exposed. Stop when the container is nearly full.
4. Harvest new potatoes after flowering by carefully feeling through the compost. For a full crop, wait until foliage yellows and dies back, then tip out the container.

Keep tubers covered so they do not turn green in light. Empty the old compost responsibly and do not plant potatoes in it again next season.

articles.title: Keeping kitchen herbs healthy in pots
articles.summary: Group herbs by water and light needs instead of treating every pot the same.
articles.body:
Most culinary herbs need good light and a pot with drainage. Rosemary, thyme and oregano prefer a free-draining mix that dries slightly between waterings. Parsley, coriander, mint and basil generally need more consistent moisture. Grow mint in its own pot because it spreads vigorously.

CHECK BEFORE WATERING
Feel the compost below the surface. Water when the mix is approaching dry for Mediterranean herbs, and before a moisture-loving herb wilts. Water the soil until a little drains out, then empty the saucer. Small pots may need checking daily in warm, windy weather.

HARVEST
Take small amounts from several stems rather than cutting one plant back severely. Pinch basil above a pair of leaves to encourage branching and remove flower buds if you want more leafy growth. Do not harvest a stressed or recently repotted plant heavily.

If leaves yellow, check drainage, watering and light before adding feed. Change one factor at a time so you can see what helps.

articles.title: Pasta with a quick tomato and garlic sauce
articles.summary: A weeknight Italian-style pantry meal with a short simmered sauce.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 10 minutes | Cooking 25 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
400 g dried pasta; 2 tablespoons olive oil; 3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; 2 x 400 g tins chopped tomatoes; 1 teaspoon dried oregano; a pinch of sugar if needed; salt and black pepper; grated hard cheese or chopped basil to serve.

METHOD
1. Boil a large pot of lightly salted water. Cook pasta to the packet time until just tender. Reserve a mug of pasta water before draining.
2. Warm olive oil in a saucepan over low heat. Add garlic and cook for about a minute until fragrant but not brown.
3. Add tomatoes and oregano. Simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens. Season to taste.
4. Toss drained pasta with the sauce. Loosen with a splash of pasta water if needed. Finish with cheese or basil.

Do not let garlic darken; burnt garlic makes the sauce bitter. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and use within 3 days.

articles.title: Irish boxty potato cakes
articles.summary: Pan-fried potato cakes combining grated raw potato with cooked mash.
articles.body:
Makes 8 small cakes | Preparation 20 minutes | Cooking 20 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
300 g floury potatoes, peeled; 250 g cold mashed potato; 100 g plain flour; 1 teaspoon baking powder; about 120 ml milk; 1 egg; 2 tablespoons butter or oil for frying; salt and black pepper.

METHOD
1. Coarsely grate the raw potatoes. Wrap in a clean tea towel and squeeze out as much liquid as you can.
2. Mix grated potato with mash, flour, baking powder, egg, salt and pepper. Add milk gradually until the thick batter holds together.
3. Heat a little butter or oil in a frying pan over medium-low heat. Spoon in small rounds and flatten gently.
4. Fry 4 to 5 minutes per side until browned and cooked through. Lower the heat if the outside colours before the centre is done. Keep finished cakes warm.

Serve with butter, eggs or a savoury meal. Cook grated-potato mixture promptly because it discolours.

articles.title: Black bean tostadas
articles.summary: Crisp tortillas topped with seasoned beans, cabbage and fresh toppings.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 15 minutes | Cooking 15 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
8 small corn tortillas; 2 x 400 g tins black beans, drained and rinsed; 1 tablespoon oil; 1 small onion, chopped; 1 teaspoon ground cumin; 100 ml water; 150 g shredded cabbage; 1 tomato, diced; 1 lime; plain yoghurt or sour cream; optional grated cheese and coriander.

METHOD
1. Heat oven to 200 C. Lay tortillas on trays and bake for 5 to 8 minutes, turning once, until crisp. Watch closely near the end.
2. Warm oil in a pan. Cook onion until soft, stir in cumin, then add beans and water. Simmer 5 minutes. Mash about half the beans to thicken; season with pepper and lime juice.
3. Spoon beans onto tortillas. Add cabbage, tomato and yoghurt, then cheese or coriander if using.

Keep crisp tortillas separate from wet toppings until serving. Refrigerate cooked beans promptly and use within 3 days.

articles.title: Simple miso soup with tofu
articles.summary: A light Japanese soup with wakame, tofu and a gently stirred miso finish.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 10 minutes | Cooking 10 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
1 litre dashi or light vegetable stock; 200 g soft or medium tofu, cubed; 1 tablespoon dried wakame; 3 to 4 tablespoons miso paste, to taste; 2 spring onions, sliced.

METHOD
1. Soak dried wakame as its packet directs, then drain.
2. Warm stock in a saucepan. Add tofu and wakame and heat gently until hot; avoid a hard boil that can break up tofu.
3. Put miso in a small bowl. Whisk in a ladle of hot stock until smooth, then stir it back into the pan. Taste and add more miso if needed.
4. Turn off the heat and add spring onions. Serve promptly.

Miso is salty, so taste before adding salt. The soup is best fresh; cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate, then reheat gently without boiling.

articles.title: Chana masala with chickpeas
articles.summary: A practical North Indian-style chickpea curry made with tinned chickpeas.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 15 minutes | Cooking 35 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
1 tablespoon oil; 1 large onion, finely chopped; 2 garlic cloves, minced; 1 teaspoon grated ginger; 1 teaspoon each ground cumin and coriander; 1/2 teaspoon turmeric; chilli powder to taste; 400 g chopped tomatoes; 2 x 400 g tins chickpeas, drained; 200 ml water; lemon juice; chopped coriander.

METHOD
1. Heat oil in a saucepan. Cook onion over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until soft and golden at the edges.
2. Add garlic, ginger and spices. Stir for 30 seconds; add a splash of water if they stick.
3. Add tomatoes and simmer 10 minutes until thickened. Stir in chickpeas and water; simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas to thicken the sauce.
4. Season with lemon juice and salt. Add coriander and serve with rice or flatbread.

Use less chilli for a milder dish. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and use within 3 days; reheat until steaming hot.

articles.title: Greek spinach and rice
articles.summary: A comforting one-pot spanakorizo finished with lemon and herbs.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 15 minutes | Cooking 35 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
2 tablespoons olive oil; 1 onion, chopped; 250 g long-grain rice, rinsed; 500 g fresh spinach or 300 g thawed and squeezed frozen spinach; 700 ml vegetable stock or water; 2 spring onions, sliced; 2 tablespoons chopped dill or parsley; 1 lemon; black pepper.

METHOD
1. Warm oil in a lidded saucepan. Cook onion for 6 to 8 minutes until soft.
2. Stir in rinsed rice and coat the grains. Add stock, bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 12 minutes.
3. Stir in spinach and spring onions. Cover and cook gently for 8 to 10 minutes until rice is tender. Add a little hot water if the pot dries before the rice is done.
4. Turn off the heat and rest covered for 5 minutes. Fold through herbs, lemon juice and black pepper.

Serve warm with yoghurt or feta if desired. Follow the rice packet if the variety needs a different liquid ratio. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and reheat thoroughly.

articles.title: Argentinian-style chimichurri
articles.summary: A fresh parsley, garlic and vinegar sauce for grilled meat or vegetables.
articles.body:
Makes about 250 ml | Preparation 15 minutes | Rest 20 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
1 packed cup finely chopped parsley; 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 1 teaspoon dried oregano; 1/2 teaspoon chilli flakes, optional; 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar; 100 ml olive oil; 2 tablespoons water; salt and black pepper.

METHOD
1. Finely chop parsley and garlic by hand; a food processor can make the sauce pasty.
2. Stir herbs, garlic, oregano, chilli if using, vinegar and water together. Rest for 10 minutes.
3. Stir in olive oil and season. Rest another 10 minutes, then adjust vinegar or seasoning.

Serve with grilled beef, chicken, vegetables or bread. This uncooked sauce does not make meat safe to eat. Refrigerate in a clean covered container and use within 3 days.

articles.title: Sort laundry and treat stains safely
articles.summary: Use garment labels and test stain treatments before applying them widely.
articles.body:
Read the care label before washing. Separate new dark colours from pale items, and separate items that need different temperatures or cycles. Empty pockets and close zips.

1. Blot fresh spills with a clean cloth; rubbing can push a stain deeper or damage fibres.
2. Check the garment label and detergent maker's stain guidance. Test treatment on an unseen area first.
3. Use cool water for unknown stains and avoid tumble drying until the mark has gone; heat can set some stains.
4. Wash at the label's recommended temperature with the correct detergent dose.

Never mix bleach with vinegar, acids, ammonia or other cleaning products. Use stain removers only as labelled, ventilate the area and keep chemicals away from children and pets.

articles.title: Reset kitchen worktops and touch points
articles.summary: Clean food-contact surfaces with a product suitable for their material.
articles.body:
Clear crumbs and food first. Wash the worktop with warm water and washing-up liquid or a cleaner labelled safe for that surface. Rinse food-contact surfaces if the label requires it. Do not use acidic cleaner on natural stone unless its maker says it is safe.

Wipe handles, taps and appliance controls with a separate clean cloth. Use food-safe sanitiser only when needed and follow its concentration and contact-time instructions. Keep raw-meat boards and cloths separate from ready-to-eat food areas.

Rinse cloths after use and let them dry fully. Replace cloths that smell or stay damp. Never mix products to make a stronger cleaner; follow the label and ventilate the room.

articles.title: Measure and mark a straight cut
articles.summary: Plan the cut, support the material and check the measurement before sawing.
articles.body:
Use a sharp pencil, tape measure, square and a saw suited to the material. Wear eye protection and secure the workpiece so it cannot move.

1. Measure from a known straight edge and mark the finished length. Check whether the saw removes material on the waste side of the line.
2. Use a square to carry the mark across the face and sides. Mark the waste piece clearly.
3. Support both sides while leaving the blade path clear. Clamp the material to a stable bench.
4. Start with a controlled shallow kerf on the waste side, then follow the line without forcing the saw. Keep hands clear.
5. Check the cut against the intended fit before making repeated pieces.

Do not cut material that may contain hidden wiring, pipes, nails or screws until it has been checked. Use power tools only if you know that model; structural work belongs with a qualified tradesperson.

articles.title: Refresh a small bathroom sealant joint
articles.summary: Remove failed sealant cleanly and use a product intended for the surface and location.
articles.body:
Use bathroom-grade sealant compatible with the surfaces, a suitable scraper, masking tape and the tools named on the package. Ventilate the room.

1. Confirm the leak is only a failed surface joint. Sealant will not repair a leaking pipe, a moving tray or water damage behind a wall.
2. Remove loose or mouldy sealant carefully without gouging the bath, tray or tiles. Follow remover instructions and clean the joint.
3. Let the joint dry fully. Mask both edges if that helps keep the bead neat.
4. Cut the nozzle to a small opening, apply a steady bead and smooth it with the tool recommended by the maker.
5. Remove masking tape and allow the full cure time on the label before exposing the joint to water.

If the substrate is damp, mould returns, or the joint keeps splitting, address the cause or ask a qualified professional. Never seal over active mould or trapped water.

articles.title: Build an even-walled pinch cup
articles.summary: Shape a small cup gradually and compress the base and rim as you work.
articles.body:
Use a small lump of well-prepared clay and a clean work surface. Keep unused clay wrapped so it does not dry.

1. Roll clay into a smooth ball. Press a thumb into the centre, stopping well above the base.
2. Rotate the ball while pinching gently between thumb and fingers. Widen the opening gradually; take small pinches rather than thinning one spot.
3. Support the outside with one hand while pressing from inside with the other. Aim for an even wall and a base thick enough to support the cup.
4. Compress the rim with damp fingers or a wooden rib. Too much water weakens the wall.
5. Set the cup on a flat board, check that it stands level, and let it firm slowly under loose plastic before trimming.

Dry and fire according to the clay and kiln makers' schedules. Do not assume a cup is food-safe until the clay, glaze fit and firing are appropriate.

articles.title: Dry a hand-built piece evenly
articles.summary: Slow, even drying reduces stress where walls, bases and handles meet.
articles.body:
Clay shrinks as it dries. A thick base attached to thin walls, or a handle that dries faster than the body, creates uneven shrinkage and can cause cracks.

1. Check that walls and base are reasonably even. Compress joins and blend attachments while clay is workable.
2. Cover the piece loosely with plastic so moisture leaves gradually. Keep it out of direct sun, draughts and direct heat.
3. Turn the piece or uncover one side at a time so air reaches it evenly. Large handles and thick joins may need to remain covered longer.
4. Inspect joins and the foot as the piece stiffens. Repair cracks while clay is workable or recycle it; slip alone will not reliably mend a deep crack.
5. Fire only when fully dry and follow the clay body and kiln manufacturer's schedule.

Drying time depends on thickness, room conditions and clay body. There is no single safe number of days for every piece.

articles.title: Back up saves before changing emulator settings
articles.summary: Keep a verified copy of save files before changing storage or emulator versions.
articles.body:
A save may depend on emulator, game region, memory-card format or title ID. Before changing settings or updating software, locate the emulator's documented save-data folder and use its export feature where available.

1. Close the game cleanly so the emulator finishes writing its save.
2. Copy the complete memory-card or save folder to a separate location. Keep the original untouched.
3. Make a second copy on another storage device if the save matters. Check copied names and sizes.
4. Test a duplicate in a separate profile if supported; do not overwrite the only working save during a test.
5. Record emulator version, game region and memory-card settings alongside the backup.

Do not use save files from untrusted sources. This guide does not identify a specific emulator's current paths; consult its upstream documentation.

articles.title: Brazilian-style rice and beans
articles.summary: A simple everyday pairing of fluffy rice with gently seasoned black beans.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 10 minutes | Cooking 35 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
250 g long-grain rice; 1 tablespoon oil; 1 small onion, finely chopped; 1 garlic clove, minced; 2 x 400 g tins black beans, drained and rinsed; 1 bay leaf; 250 ml water or stock; salt and black pepper; chopped parsley, optional.

METHOD
1. Warm half the oil in a saucepan. Add half the onion and cook until soft. Stir in the rice until coated, then add 500 ml water and a pinch of salt. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on low for 12 to 15 minutes, until tender. Rest covered for 5 minutes.
2. Meanwhile, heat the remaining oil in another pan. Cook the rest of the onion until soft, then stir in garlic for 30 seconds.
3. Add beans, bay leaf and 250 ml water or stock. Simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes. Mash a few beans to thicken the liquid; season with pepper and salt. Remove the bay leaf.
4. Serve the beans alongside rice, with parsley if desired.

For a smoky flavour, add a little smoked paprika; it is a variation rather than a substitute for a traditional seasoning. Cool leftovers promptly, refrigerate and use within 3 days. Reheat until steaming hot.

articles.title: Record Android version and build details
articles.summary: Capture exact software and model details before troubleshooting a device.
articles.body:
Before changing an Android device, record manufacturer, exact model number, Android version, build number, security patch level and carrier or region variant. Similar names can refer to different hardware.

Find details in Settings under About phone or About tablet; wording varies by manufacturer. Do not share IMEI, serial number, account email or unlock codes publicly.

Before a major update, reset, bootloader change or repair, back up important photos, documents and authenticator recovery information. Confirm that you can access the backup. Read the device maker's support page and exact model instructions.

Rooting, unlocking and installing a custom ROM can erase data, affect security updates, break banking or DRM features and make a device unusable. Compatibility changes over time; check current maintainer guidance for your exact build.

articles.title: Spotting and responding to potato and tomato blight
articles.summary: Recognise fast-spreading late blight symptoms and reduce the chance of carrying infected material through the garden.
articles.body:
Blight is a fast-moving disease of potatoes and tomatoes that is favoured by mild, wet weather. Symptoms can resemble other plant problems, so treat this as a first inspection rather than a definitive diagnosis.

LOOK FOR
Check leaves, stems and fruit after wet spells. Warning signs include rapidly spreading watery patches that turn brown, collapsing leaves, dark stem lesions and brown, rotting tomato fruit. A fine pale growth may appear at lesion edges in humid conditions. Greenhouse leaf mould can look similar on leaves.

WHAT TO DO
1. Inspect both sides of leaves and stems. Photograph the whole plant and close details for comparison with a trusted local horticultural source.
2. Remove a few affected leaves carefully; this may slow spread but does not cure infection. Clean hands and tools before moving to another plant.
3. If symptoms spread rapidly, remove badly affected material and keep it out of a cool home compost heap. Follow local council disposal guidance.
4. Check nearby potatoes and tomatoes often. Space plants for airflow, water the soil rather than foliage and avoid handling wet plants.
5. Inspect produce at harvest; do not store visibly rotting fruit or tubers. Remove volunteer potatoes in following seasons and rotate crops where practical.

TROUBLESHOOTING AND MISTAKES
Brown leaf marks without rapid spread can have other causes; monitor new growth and seek a second opinion. A greenhouse does not guarantee protection. Do not assume one removed leaf means the plant is clear. Do not use a pesticide unless it is currently authorised for home gardeners in your jurisdiction and its label covers the crop.

REFERENCE
RHS Advice: Tomato blight — https://www.rhs.org.uk/disease/tomato-blight

articles.title: Watering containers and raised beds evenly
articles.summary: Check moisture at root level and water slowly enough to reach the whole root ball.
articles.body:
Pots and raised beds can dry faster than open ground because more growing mix is exposed to wind and sun. A fixed daily schedule may leave roots alternately dry and waterlogged. Check the mix and plant instead.

METHOD
1. Check below the surface near the edge and near the plant. A dry crust can hide damp compost; a wet surface can hide a dry root ball. Lift a small pot to compare its weight after watering and as it dries.
2. Water slowly across the surface until water drains from the base. If very dry compost repels water, apply a little, wait, then water again.
3. Empty standing water from saucers and keep drainage holes clear.
4. Recheck during warm, windy weather and when crops are fruiting or forming roots. Seedlings need closer attention than established plants.
5. Where practical, water soil in the morning and avoid wetting foliage on disease-prone plants.

EXAMPLES AND TROUBLESHOOTING
A small sunny herb pot may need checking often; a large shaded tub may stay moist longer. Lettuce, potatoes and cauliflower are sensitive to drought at key stages, while many Mediterranean herbs prefer the mix to dry somewhat between waterings. Midday wilting can be heat stress, so check soil before watering again. Yellow leaves in persistently wet compost may point to poor drainage.

COMMON MISTAKES
Do not give every plant the same schedule. Avoid a quick splash that wets only the top layer or leaving a container in a full tray.

REFERENCE
RHS Advice: Watering vegetables and fruit — https://www.rhs.org.uk/vegetables/watering

articles.title: Plan a safe wall fixing before drilling
articles.summary: Identify the wall, choose a suitable fixing and check for concealed services before making a hole.
articles.body:
A safe fixing starts with knowing the wall material and likely load. Plasterboard, masonry and timber need different fixings. Heavy, overhead or safety-critical loads require suitable hardware and a sound substrate; ask a competent tradesperson if unsure.

TOOLS
Tape measure, pencil, spirit level, drill and bit suited to the wall, rated fixing, eye protection and a quality cable/metal detector. Use an RCD with portable power tools where required by their instructions.

METHOD
1. Check the item's instructions and estimate its loaded weight. Identify the wall material at an existing opening or with a detector.
2. Choose a fixing whose package covers the wall type and load. Follow its pilot-hole diameter and depth.
3. Inspect the other side of the wall and locate sockets, switches and pipes. Scan with a suitable detector, but treat it as an aid rather than proof that an area is clear.
4. If drilling near electrical equipment, isolate the relevant circuit only when safe and within your competence. Do not do electrical work yourself. Stop if cables or pipes cannot be ruled out.
5. Mark level points, wear eye protection and drill with the specified bit and depth. Insert the fixing without forcing it, secure the bracket and load gradually.

TROUBLESHOOTING
A plug that spins may mean the hole is oversized or the wall unsuitable; stop and reassess. Crumbling plaster is not a sound anchor. Never drill through uncertainty.

REFERENCE
Electrical Safety First: DIY safety advice — https://www.electricalsafetyfirst.org.uk/safety-advice/home-and-people/diy-ers/

articles.title: Use household cleaners safely and never mix products
articles.summary: Read the label, ventilate the room and use one cleaning product at a time.
articles.body:
Household cleaners can irritate or burn skin and eyes, and incompatible products can release harmful gases. Never mix cleaning products, including bleach with acids such as vinegar or toilet cleaner, or with ammonia-containing products.

BEFORE YOU START
Read the full label and hazard symbols. Check surface compatibility, prepare ventilation, keep children and pets away, and use the protective equipment named by the manufacturer. Keep the product in its original labelled container.

SAFE ROUTINE
1. Remove loose dirt with water and detergent where suitable. Use only the amount and dilution stated on the label.
2. Apply one product at a time. Follow its contact time, rinsing and ventilation instructions.
3. Never transfer chemicals to a drinks bottle or unlabelled jar. Close containers after use and store them out of reach.
4. Rinse food-contact surfaces if the label directs and wash hands after cleaning.
5. If someone has breathing trouble, eye exposure, burns or feels unwell, move to fresh air if safe and contact emergency services or a poison information service.

COMMON MISTAKES
Do not combine products to make them stronger; do not use bleach on surfaces unless its label permits it; never pour a new cleaner into a bottle containing another product. If a product damages a surface, stop, ventilate and follow label guidance for rinsing.

REFERENCE
UK HSE cleaning-products guidance — https://www.hse.gov.uk/chemical-classification/labelling-packaging/cleaning-products-and-corrosive-pictogram.htm

articles.title: Prepare an old phone for reuse or recycling
articles.summary: Back up what matters, protect account access and use a suitable reuse or e-waste route.
articles.body:
Before passing on or recycling a phone, protect personal data and use an appropriate collection route. Reset menus and account-removal steps vary by maker, model and Android version; follow the exact manufacturer's current instructions.

PREPARE
1. Check that photos, contacts, documents and authenticator recovery methods are backed up. Open the backup elsewhere to confirm it is usable.
2. Record the exact model and note any faults. Do not share an IMEI, serial number or recovery code publicly.
3. For reuse, follow the maker's steps to remove personal accounts and removable storage, then perform its documented factory reset. Confirm the welcome screen appears and do not sign in again with your personal account.
4. Remove SIM and memory cards. Tell the recipient about faults and battery condition.
5. If it cannot be reused, take it to an authorised electrical-waste or battery collection point. WEEE Ireland lists recycling centres, participating retailers and collection events.

BATTERY SAFETY
Do not puncture, crush, dismantle or bin a phone battery. If it is swollen, hot, leaking or damaged, stop charging or using it and ask the manufacturer or authorised waste site how to handle it. Do not place a damaged battery into a public collection box without checking its guidance.

TROUBLESHOOTING
If backup is incomplete, keep the old phone until you choose what to do with missing data. If setup asks for the prior account after reset, stop and follow the manufacturer's account-removal process rather than handing it over as ready to use.

REFERENCE
WEEE Ireland: where to recycle household electrical items — https://www.weeeireland.ie/household-recycling/where-can-i-recycle/
